en.title: Haymitch's Painful Truth: 'Sunrise on the Reaping' Dives Deep into Propaganda
en.summary: Suzanne Collins's new Hunger Games prequel, 'Sunrise on the Reaping,' is set to explore the devastating story of Haymitch Abernathy and the 50th Hunger Games. The novel promises a searing look at the mechanics of misinformation, a theme that resonates deeply with our current reality.
en.body:
The world of Panem is about to get a lot more personal, and perhaps, a lot more uncomfortable. **Suzanne Collins** is returning to the universe that captivated millions with **'Sunrise on the Reaping,'** a prequel novel set a full 24 years before Katniss Everdeen's rebellion. This latest installment will delve into the harrowing backstory of **Haymitch Abernathy**, the jaded but ultimately crucial mentor from the original trilogy, during his own brutal Hunger Games experience.

Set against the backdrop of the 50th Hunger Games, often referred to as the Second Quarter Quell, the novel promises to unpack the insidious nature of propaganda. Collins herself has stated that she was inspired by philosopher David Hume's observations on how easily the masses are governed by the few. This theme of implicit submission, coupled with the power of those who control the narrative, feels particularly urgent in our current age. The question Collins posed with the original series, 'Real or not real?', seems to echo even louder now, as the lines between truth and manufactured reality blur daily.

> "They will not use my tears for their entertainment." — Haymitch Abernathy

This poignant quote, attributed to Haymitch in the upcoming novel, encapsulates the profound personal toll of the Games and the Capitol's manipulative entertainment. It speaks to a resistance, not of open rebellion, but of a refusal to let one's suffering be commodified for the pleasure of others. The promotional push for **'Sunrise on the Reaping,'** much like previous adaptations, has already ignited passionate discussions online. As Sophie Hanson noted in Junkee, the discourse surrounding these new entries can sometimes mirror the very scenes from the story itself, highlighting how deeply the themes of Panem have infiltrated our own societal consciousness.

## The Ever-Present Echo of Panem

The anticipation for **'Sunrise on the Reaping'** is palpable, especially among the dedicated fanbase who have followed **The Hunger Games** saga for years. This novel isn't just another prequel; it's an opportunity to understand the origins of the cynicism and resilience that defined Haymitch. For fans, it represents a chance to revisit the world that so brilliantly satirized political manipulation and societal control, and to see those themes amplified through the eyes of a character who lived them so intimately. The resonance between the fictional Capitol's control over information and real-world struggles with misinformation creates a powerful, almost unsettling, connection.

## What's Next

**'Sunrise on the Reaping'** is slated for release in November 2026. Fans can expect a deep dive into Haymitch's past and the chilling mechanics of the 50th Hunger Games. Further details regarding potential adaptations or related media have not yet been announced.

content_raw: Chances are you’ve seen promotion for the November 20 release of Sunrise on the Reaping . The adaptation of Suzanne Collins’s 2025 book of the same name is a prequel set 24 years before the events of The Hunger Games . Taking place during the 50th Hunger Games, it provides the backstory of Haymitch Abernathy, a major figure in the rest of the series. Although propaganda has been a key theme throughout the blockbuster series, Sunrise puts a laser focus on our modern age of misinformation . “I was inspired by David Hume’s idea of implicit submission and, in his words, ‘the easiness with which the many are governed by the few,’” Collins said in a statement when the book was first announced back in 2024. “The story also lent itself to a deeper dive into the use of propaganda and the power of those who control the narrative. The question ‘Real or not real?’ seems more pressing to me every day.” Sophie Hanson at Junkee writes about the repeated discourse that arises online whenever the franchise sees a new adaptation. It’s a worthwhile read, especially for its searing final line: “It’s worth noticing when the way we talk about the story starts to look less like a response to it and more like a scene from it.” It’s hard not to feel like living in America is living in Panem. But even beyond the ways American politics have all but sent children to a bloody battle for citizen entertainment (err, ignoring The Patriot Games and whatever came of that), the promotional push for Sunrise , as in film adaptations of the franchise before, feels as though we’re in the story itself. Capita(o)lism is the name of the game, and good little consumers–us–flock to the franchise’s offerings. It’s hard not to when pop culture and consumer favorites get the Hunger Games treatment. Taking inspiration from the prequel’s title, Diff eyewear and the film have teamed up to offer four different sunglasses inspired by the lead characters . You can snag ray protection honoring Effie (“iconic and elegant”), Snow (“sleek and structured”), Haymitch (“classic and cool”), or Lenore Dove (“strong and sweet”). Before you don those specs, though, glamorize your eyes with the Stila x Sunrise collaborative makeup offerings (Stila is “the official makeup partner” for the film). Find eyeshadows, eye liner, highlighter, and all-over glitter to create “epic looks.” And never fear what the people of Panem may smell like. You can know, thanks to the collaboration between Jukebox and Sunrise . That’s not to touch upon Sunrise on the Reaping ’s powerhouse soundtrack, with a who’s who of long-time and contemporary favorites comprising its tracklist. Soundtracks have been gaining in popularity again after falling off in the 2010s, and it’s hard not to see the rumors, speculation, and excitement over Sunrise ’s as reminiscent of the excitement of film soundtracks . . . 24 years ago, an era of many of our own origin stories .
